scenes.tts: Under the best laboratory conditions, one E. coli cell can split into two about every 20 minutes. A cold sore can heal, then come back later in about the same spot. How do bacteria and viruses make more of themselves, and why do some infections come back years later?
scenes.visual: A bacterium splits in two on a 20-minute clock; a cold sore heals and returns at the same patch of skin; the question appears under both
scenes.narration: Under the best laboratory conditions, one E. coli cell can split into two about every 20 minutes. A cold sore can heal, then come back later in about the same spot. How do bacteria and viruses make more of themselves, and why do some infections come back years later?

scenes.tts: Most bacteria reproduce by binary fission. One cell grows, copies its D N A, and splits into two cells. Each new cell gets a complete copy of the chromosome, so the two are usually identical. Conjugation is different. One cell passes a plasmid, a small extra circle of D N A, to another. There are still two cells, but one has new genes.
scenes.visual: Binary fission in four steps, then conjugation: a plasmid chip moves between two cells, still two cells

scenes.tts: Doubling time is how long a population takes to double. Take a model population of 100 cells that doubles every 20 minutes. Two hours is six doublings, so 100 cells become 6,400. From one E. coli cell, 21 doublings, or seven hours, give more than two million cells. These are calculated numbers, not counts.
scenes.visual: Number line of cells doubling six times with x2 arrows, then one cell to 2,097,152 labelled calculated
scenes.narration: Doubling time is how long a population takes to double. Take a model population of 100 cells that doubles every 20 minutes. Two hours is six doublings, so 100 cells become 6,400. From one E. coli cell, 21 doublings, or seven hours, give more than two million cells. These are calculated numbers, not counts.

scenes.tts: The model assumes no cells die, no waiting, and endless food. Real cultures differ. First comes a lag, when the count barely rises. Then comes fast growth, close to steady doubling. Last, food runs low and wastes build up, so growth levels off.
scenes.visual: A sketch plot: dashed endless-doubling line, then the real-culture curve with lag, fast growth and levelling off stages

scenes.tts: A virus cannot split, grow, or make anything on its own. It needs a host cell, the living cell it infects. A bacteriophage, or phage, infects bacteria. In the lytic cycle, the phage injects its D N A. The host copies it and builds viral parts. New phages are assembled. The cell bursts, the new phages escape, and the host cell dies.
scenes.visual: A phage attaches to a bacterium and injects DNA; viral parts and new phages appear inside; the cell bursts and phages escape

scenes.tts: In the lysogenic cycle, the viral D N A joins the host's own D N A. This stored D N A is called a prophage. Each time the bacterium divides, both daughter cells get a copy. Later, damage to the cell's D N A can switch the prophage into the lytic cycle. The herpes virus behind cold sores also stays in sensory nerve cells, and from time to time becomes active again. A virus never divides. A host cell builds it, right away or later.
scenes.visual: Prophage in the chromosome, passed to two daughters, switch to lytic; a nerve-cell block with a hidden virus that wakes; the rule
